claims.text: The starting refractory HEA is an as-cast, homogeneous, single-phase material with a uniform microstructure.
Immersion in molten Cu at approximately 1150–1200 °C for 72–96 hours will permit selective element extraction and Cu infiltration.
Liquid-metal dealloying will create aligned, interpenetrating Cu channels within a continuous HEA matrix.
The Cu channels produced by the treatment will be nearly pure and bicontinuous.
Passivating element segregation may form at Cu/HEA interfaces and stabilize those interfaces.
Selective extraction of relatively reactive HEA elements causes local dissolution at interdendritic regions.
Local dissolution enables molten Cu to infiltrate the HEA and form continuous channels.
The residual HEA ligaments become enriched in refractory elements having low Cu solubility.
The residual refractory-element-rich HEA ligaments retain high strength and thermal stability.
Continuous Cu pathways enhance effective heat conduction through the treated material.
The continuous HEA network supports mechanical integrity under irradiation and thermal loading.
The treated material will have substantially higher thermal conductivity than the untreated HEA, particularly at elevated operating temperatures.
The treated material will maintain the HEA matrix's high-temperature strength.
The treated material will maintain the HEA matrix's irradiation resistance.
The untreated as-cast HEA has relatively lower thermal conductivity and lacks engineered HEA/Cu connectivity.
The proposed benefits should hold primarily above approximately 650 °C and under plasma-like irradiation conditions.
Departures from optimized dealloying parameters may cause over-dealloying or detrimental phase segregation that compromises mechanical properties.
